From the fallen bough come the forest's ways: the edge-folk trade only in deadwood; a Reeve speaks for the ents and is punished if he speaks for himself; the timber that Kilinti's charter owes the crown is paid in what the wind brings down; and the ents remember the one time they acted quickly, when the Black Roots of the Necromancer crept up the valley in 3A 780 and they walked to the eastern edge and pulled the dead roots out of the ground with their hands, after which the forest was silent for a year.

sign.device: A fallen oak bough lying across the field, leaved and bearing acorns, brown and green on pale gold.
sign.origin: The bough is the one the eldest oak let fall before Aen's envoy in 1A 77, the ents' whole answer to the kingdom's request for timber. The Reeves keep a piece of its wood in the moot-grove at Ollolor and carry a painted bough before them when they speak for the forest in Parim, and every timber-bill the edge-folk sell is sealed with a fallen branch, never a standing tree.
sign.meaning: We give what falls and nothing that stands. To the crown it promises timber without end on the forest's terms; to anyone who brings an axe to a standing tree it says the bargain is ended, and the edge-folk know that the ents remember the Great Felling the Eldest refused.

dynasties.name: The Eldest of the Moot
dynasties.notable: The ents have no line: the Eldest is whichever of them has said the fewest words in the year, and the Eldest speaks last at the Ent-Moot every seventh spring. The edge-folk call the present Eldest Gronnar.

dynasties.name: The Edge-Reeves
dynasties.notable: Since the Timber Bargain the men of the edge-villages elect a Reeve to keep the forest's accounts and to sit in Parim for it; the Reeves are the only lords of Kilinti a man ever sees.

events.name: The Timber Bargain
events.summary: Aen's kingdom asks the forest for its oaks; the Ent-Moot answers, after three springs, that the kingdom may have every tree that falls of itself and none that stands, and the bargain has held for four ages.

events.name: The Reeve Who Spoke for Himself
events.summary: A Reeve sells standing oaks in the forest's name; the ents walk to his village, the edge-folk give him up to the moot-grove, and no Reeve has spoken for himself since.

events.name: The Dead Roots Turned
events.summary: When the Black Roots creep up the Aenar valley, the ents walk to the forest's eastern edge and pull the dead roots out of the ground by hand; the edge-folk say the forest was silent for a year afterwards.

events.name: The Grove Charter
events.summary: Kilinti takes the Charters of Parim with two seats, one for the grove and one for the edge, and the charter asks of it only timber.

events.name: The Great Felling Refused
events.summary: Parim asks for standing oaks to roof the new halls of the lake ports; the Eldest's answer, carried by the Reeve, is a single word, and the king does not ask again.

countries.capitalReason: Ollolor is the moot-grove in the oldest part of the forest, where the ents gather every seventh spring; it has no walls and no houses, and the Reeves' hall stands at the forest edge a day's walk away because men may not sleep in the grove.
countries.today: Kilinti in 4A 1748 is a chartered dominion of a few thousand ents and some 72,000 edge-folk, holding two charter-seats. The ents keep the forest, the men keep the accounts and the timber trade in fallen wood, and the Golden Court has never found anything in Kilinti it could sell.

divergence.what: The Ent-Moot, called out of season, walks out of the forest against an army that burns its edge.
divergence.consequence: Whatever army it is learns what the Black Roots learned, and the Concord learns that its slowest dominion is not its weakest.

divergence.what: The Eldest closes the forest to every army, the crown's included, for the length of the war.
divergence.consequence: The upper Aenar becomes a wall in the middle of the Vale, and the Host must march around a dominion that has chosen no side.

countries.name: Safeton

founding.story: The lake bargemen who carried the Vale's grain down the Safen to the sea built their warehouses at the river mouth where lake water and sea water meet, and the town of Lotrenri grew round them. The ship-houses that owned the warehouses came to rule the town between them, and the harbour has been governed by a council of ship-houses since the Second Age, the only dominion of the Concord with no lord at all.

roots.story: Safeton's people are bargemen before they are anything else. The Safen is the Great Lake's only outflow, and long before Aen the barge-folk who poled the lake's grain down it to the sea were their own small people of boats, with a custom the ship-houses still keep: at the river mouth, where the lake's sweet water meets the salt, every barge pours one bucket of lake water into the sea at the spring sailing, so that the lake will know where its children have gone. The ship-houses that owned the warehouses at the mouth grew from barge-families, and the harbour has had no lord since the Grey Breath of 2A 410 killed the crown's governor and the ship-houses ran the town through the plague and would not give it back. Their whole craft is the craft of surviving masters. When Elzon's Order took the Vale, the ship-houses sank their best hulls in the Safen mud, raised them on moonless nights to smuggle for the Isle Houses and sank them again before dawn, and for nine centuries and more the Order taxed a harbour of rotten fishing boats. From that comes the harbour's character: no lord, because a lord can be made to give up his ships; council votes taken by hull, not by house; a contempt for anything that cannot float; and the knowledge, taught to every ship-house child, of where in the mud the hulls once lay.

sign.device: A black ship's hull, keel upward, rising out of a mud-brown base, on pale sea-green.
sign.origin: The keel-up hull is a sunken ship rising from the Safen mud, the sign the smugglers of the Order's centuries chalked on the doors of houses that had a hull in the river. When the Order fell in 3A 1260 the ship-houses raised every hidden hull on one tide and sailed them into Lotrenri under the chalked sign, and the Council of Ship-Houses has flown it over the harbour since.
sign.meaning: We go under and come up again. It promises the harbour that no master can take what the river hides, and tells any lord who would rule Safeton that the ships will be under the mud before his men reach the quays.

dynasties.name: The Council of Ship-Houses
dynasties.notable: The heads of the ship-houses of Lotrenri sit as the council and choose a Harbour-Master each year from among themselves; the oldest houses, Lotaren and Safarel, have between them provided half the Harbour-Masters in the harbour's history.

events.name: The Lake Water Poured Out
events.summary: The barge-folk of the Safen pour one bucket of lake water into the sea at every spring sailing so the lake will know where its children have gone; the ship-houses still keep the custom.

events.name: The Ship-Houses Take the Town
events.summary: When the crown's governor dies of the Grey Breath, the ship-houses run the harbour through the plague and refuse to give it back; Parim, with no one else to send, confirms them.

events.name: The Hidden Hulls
events.summary: Under the Order the ship-houses sink their best hulls in the Safen mud and raise them for smuggling on moonless nights; the Isle Houses buy what they carry.

events.name: The Hulls Raised on One Tide
events.summary: As the Order falls, the ship-houses raise every hull hidden in the Safen mud on a single tide and sail them into Lotrenri under the chalked sign of the keel-up hull.

events.name: Novez Joins the Harbour
events.summary: The farmers of the Novez Fields, chartered separately in 4A 3, sell their seat's levy to the ship-houses in a famine year and become part of the harbour dominion, which keeps both seats.

events.name: The Grain Wars Profit
events.summary: When the Gunwyn and Girdon wars divide the West Lands, Safeton sells grain to both sides and builds its new mole with the profit.

rivalries.nature: The lake road and the river road compete for the same grain, and the spring-town's Golden Charter freed its carts from tolls that Safeton's barges still pay.

countries.capitalReason: Lotrenri stands at the Safen mouth, where the Great Lake's only outflow meets the sea: everything the Vale sends south by water passes its quays, and the bar at the mouth makes it the one harbour the lake ships and the sea ships can share.
countries.today: Safeton in 4A 1748 is the Concord's southern harbour, a dominion of some 1.11 million ruled by its council of ship-houses and holding the charter-seats of Safeton and Novez. Its ships carry grain to every coast and pilgrims south over the Sea of Peace, and its Harbour-Master has more ships than the crown.

divergence.what: When the western fleets cross, the ship-houses open Lotrenri to them in exchange for keeping their warehouses.
divergence.consequence: The West gains a southern harbour and a road up the Safen to the lake, and the Concord learns what a dominion with no lord will do for its trade.

divergence.what: The council lends every hull it has to the crown's fleet before the Crossing.
divergence.consequence: Aenor's fleet can meet the West at sea, and the harbour stakes its trade on a crown that may not survive.

countries.name: Freshon

founding.story: A warm spring rises where the lake road meets the south road, and a spring-house of Sulethe stood over it before there was a town. Travellers stopped to drink and drovers to water their herds, the drovers' inns became a market, and the market became Hordorton, the spring-town, whose spring-masters have governed it under one charter or another since the First Age.

roots.story: The warm spring of Hordorton is older than any name the drovers gave it, and the drovers of the south road tell how it was found: long before Aen, in a summer of drought, a drover's ox, dying of thirst at the crossing of the roads, went down on its knees and struck the ground with its horn, and warm water came up where it knelt. The drovers buried the ox beside the water and set its horns over the spring, and the first spring-house of Sulethe was raised over the grave before there was a town. The spring-masters' customs come from that kneeling: whoever comes to the spring is given water before he is asked his business, ox or king; no beast is slaughtered within sight of the spring-house; a drover's ox is watered free; and the masters bow when they draw water, because the spring was given to a creature on its knees. The water's healing was proved in the fever years of 2A 640, when the sick who drank only from the spring died less often than the rest, and the spring-houses became the hospitals of the southern Vale. That gift has its other side. Freshon has always served whoever came, and in 4A 1731 the spring-masters knelt to the Golden King for a Golden Charter at a price that emptied three generations of savings, which Pazoma's guild-masters never tire of mentioning.

sign.device: A white ox kneeling, on a field of warm red-brown.
sign.origin: The kneeling ox is the drovers' ox that found the spring, whose horns hung over the first spring-house until demon raiders burned the house in 2A 1240 and the horns were lost. The spring-masters had the kneeling ox carved over the new door and painted on the carts that carried the sick to the spring-houses, and in fever years a cart bearing the kneeling ox was let through every closed road of the southern Vale.
sign.meaning: Water before questions, and healing for any who come. It promises every traveller that he will be served at the spring; its rivals read it as a town that kneels to whoever pays, and the Golden Charter has made the joke sharper in 4A 1748.

dynasties.name: The Spring-Masters
dynasties.notable: The town is ruled by a council of the spring-masters, the families who hold the leases on the spring-houses and the inns round the spring; the First Spring-Master is chosen by lot from the council every third year.

events.name: The Ox at the Crossing
events.summary: A drover's ox dying of thirst at the crossing of the roads kneels and strikes the ground, and warm water rises; the drovers bury the ox beside the spring and set its horns over the water.

events.name: The Fever Wells
events.summary: In a fever year the physicians of the southern Vale find that the sick who drink only from the warm spring die less often than the rest; Freshon's spring-houses become the hospitals of the southern Vale.

events.name: The Horns Lost
events.summary: Demon raiders out of the southern gates burn the first spring-house and the ox's horns are lost; the masters carve the kneeling ox over the door of the house they raise in its place.

events.name: The Two Seats
events.summary: Freshon takes the Charters of Parim with two seats, because its markets owe the common defence more carts and horses than most dominions.

events.name: The Golden Charter
events.summary: The spring-masters buy a Golden Charter from the King, which frees their carts from royal tolls and gives the town its own court, at a price that empties three generations of savings.

rivalries.nature: Both bought Golden Charters and each says the other paid too little; their quarrel over the lake road tolls has gone to the Concord court four times since 4A 1734.
The spring-town's carts and the harbour's barges carry the same grain by different roads.

countries.capitalReason: Hordorton is the spring itself: the warm water where the lake road meets the south road, which made every traveller stop and so made a market where there would otherwise have been a ford.
countries.today: Freshon in 4A 1748 is a chartered spring-town of some 1.25 million in its town and four states of spring country, holding two charter-seats and the Golden Charter it bought in 4A 1731. Its spring-masters are proud, indebted and loyal to the Golden Court, because the Golden Court holds their debts.

divergence.what: A new ruler in Parim revokes the Golden Charters.
divergence.consequence: Freshon's spring-masters lose the price they paid and their loyalty with it, and the Golden Court loses its surest dominion.

divergence.what: In the war the spring-houses of Freshon become the hospitals of the Host.
divergence.consequence: The spring-town's wells keep an army alive, and the spring-masters ask a seat at whatever council follows the war.

countries.name: Pazoma

founding.story: The deep bay of Horlomon on the lake shore could take any ship the lake carried, and the craftsmen who settled round it in the First Age, bell-founders, glass-blowers, cloth-dyers and paper-makers, ruled the town through their guilds from the beginning. Pazoma has never had a lord; its guild-masters sit as its council, and its charter has always been written in their name.

roots.story: Pazoma began as a mercy. In the last years of the War of Men the craftsmen of the beaten kings, smiths, glass-blowers, dyers and the rest, were gathered at the deep bay of Horlomon by victors who had no use for craftsmen bound to dead crowns, and the guilds' own chronicle says they were spared on one condition: that they make things for the peace and none for war. When Aen's Peace of the One Crown forbade the lords to make war on one another, the crown took up the lords' surplus swords, and in 1A 410 the seven guilds of the bay bought the whole hoard by weight and melted it into the guild-hall bell, the largest ever cast in the Middle Lands, with one blade kept whole for its clapper. From the bell come Horlomon's laws and pride: no guild of the bay forges a weapon, though its glass, paper and cloth go to every army of the Concord; the bell rings for every guild election, every charter and every wrong the town will not bear, as it rang for three days in the Bell Riot of 4A 1610; the town has never had a lord, because its craftsmen were the beaten kings' and swore never to serve one again; and the paper-makers' conviction, proved under the Order when they hid the kingdom's books in the guild cellars, that a city of craft outlives a city of soldiers.

sign.device: A bronze bell whose clapper is a sword-blade, gold on deep blue.
sign.origin: The bell is the guild-hall bell of Horlomon, cast in 1A 410 from the swords the Peace of the One Crown took from the lords, with one blade left whole to strike it. The paper-makers printed it inside every book they hid under the Order, so that the books could be found again, and the guild council flies it over the hall whenever the bell is rung.
sign.meaning: The sword serves the bell. It promises that Horlomon makes for the peace and rings against any wrong; to the Golden Court it recalls the Bell Riot, and to an enemy it says that the town will ring before it yields.

dynasties.name: The Guild-Masters of Horlomon
dynasties.notable: The masters of the seven great guilds sit as the council and choose a Warden of the Guilds each year; the bell-founders have always held the first seat, because the bell of the guild hall rang the town into existence.

events.name: The Craftsmen of the Beaten Kings
events.summary: Craftsmen of the kings beaten in the War of Men are gathered at the bay of Horlomon and spared on condition that they make for the peace and never for war.

events.name: The Seven Guilds
events.summary: The bell-founders, glass-blowers, dyers, paper-makers, bookbinders, rope-makers and shipwrights of the bay swear one council and cast the guild-hall bell.

events.name: The Hidden Presses
events.summary: Under the Order the paper-makers and bookbinders hide the kingdom's books in the guild cellars, and the printers' saying is still that Pazoma kept Aenor's memory while the Necromancer kept its body.

events.name: The Marked Books
events.summary: The paper-makers print the sword-clappered bell inside every book they hide in the guild cellars so that the books can be found again; Pazoma's libraries still shelve them first.

events.name: The Bell Riot
events.summary: When the crown's tax on bells doubles, the bell-founders ring every bell in the town for three days and nights until the Royal Council rescinds it; the riot is the guild-city's proudest memory.

events.name: The Golden Charter
events.summary: The guild council buys a Golden Charter from the King, three years after Freshon, and pays more for it, which Horlomon has not forgiven.

rivalries.nature: Rivals for the Golden Court's favour and the lake road's tolls since both bought Golden Charters.

countries.capitalReason: Horlomon stands on the deepest bay of the Great Lake's shore, where ships of any draught can lie at the quays and the guild workshops can load bells, glass and books straight onto them.
countries.today: Pazoma in 4A 1748 is a chartered guild-city of some 1.25 million in its town and lake shore, holding two charter-seats and the Golden Charter it bought in 4A 1734. It makes the Concord's bells, glass, cloth, paper and books, and its guild-masters keep the best library outside the universities.

divergence.what: The guild presses print the stranger's warnings and the scholars' doubts in the year of the King's death.
divergence.consequence: Every lake town reads what the Royal Council would rather it did not, and the Golden Charter will not save the guilds if the wrong camp wins.

divergence.what: When the heir returns, Horlomon rings every bell it has for him.
divergence.consequence: The guild-city declares for him before any lord does, and the lake shore follows its bells.

countries.name: Orohaf

founding.story: Aenor Isle had five great houses, Orohaf, Rish, Tinta, Holod and Faber, each ruled by its eldest woman, and in the year the chroniclers give their eldest women met at the harbour of Borrak and swore the Tide-Oath: one queen chosen from among them for life, the isle's ships at her call, and the dead given to the tide by the same rite in every house. The isle has been a queenship ever since, and its houses still choose the queen in the tide-chamber at the turn of the tide.

roots.story: The Isle Houses are what is left of the Water clan of the Low Country. When the plain still lay where the Crown Sea is now, Aenor Isle and the Tinta Hills were its eastern heights, and the Water clan's cord-mothers kept the harbours and sluices of the plain's eastern edge. On the Night of the Sea the eldest woman of the clan steered the last boat out of the drowning streets, standing at the steering-oar through the whole night until the tide turned at dawn, and brought it to the heights with the clan's mothers aboard; the five daughters' lines of that boat became the houses of Orohaf, Rish, Tinta, Holod and Faber. They lost the Orran tongue in the centuries after and kept everything else of the Low Country's last law: the eldest women rule; the dead are given to the tide that took the land; and the queen of the isle is chosen in the tide-chamber at the turn of the tide, the hour the steerswoman's boat touched the heights, when the queen-to-be takes the steering-oar of her house and holds it until the water stands still. Every isle child learns to dive before it learns its letters, and the old divers of Borrak say that at the lowest spring tides a mound breaks the water west of the isle, and that the houses have always known what lies under it and have never dived for it. Whether that is true, the tide-mothers will not say.

sign.device: A white steering-oar standing upright, blade down, on a field of sea-blue over black.
sign.origin: The oar is the steering-oar the Water clan's eldest woman held through the Night of the Sea, and every queen since has been chosen by taking her house's oar in the tide-chamber at the turn of the tide and holding it until the water stands still. When the five eldest women swore the Tide-Oath at Borrak in 1A 133, they set five oars upright in the harbour mud with the queen's in the middle, and the isle's ships have flown the white oar since.
sign.meaning: We steered through the night the land drowned. It promises that the queen keeps the isle's course and that any fleet crossing from the West must pass the oar; to the Veiled and the Redbark it says that the Isle Houses still keep the last law of the drowned country, and that the tide-mothers remember whose the sea once was.

dynasties.name: The Queens of the Five Houses
dynasties.notable: The queen is chosen by the eldest women of the five houses from among the daughters of any of them, and her house holds the harbour of Borrak for her life; inheritance on the isle runs through daughters. Queen Faberra, of the house of Faber, reigns in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Steerswoman's Night
events.summary: On the Night of the Sea the eldest woman of the Water clan steers the last boat out of the drowning streets and holds the oar until the tide turns; the five Isle Houses descend from the daughters aboard.

events.name: The Last Law of the Low Country
events.summary: The isle houses keep the custom of the drowned plain without its tongue: their eldest women rule, their queen is chosen in the tide-chamber at the turn of the tide, and their dead are given to the tide.

events.name: The Refugee Ships
events.summary: In the famine centuries the Isle Houses take in shiploads of Vale families and give them the green heart of Rish to farm; the isle's grandmothers say the tide brought them.

events.name: The Timber Fleet
events.summary: Isle House ships, sailing south in a storm year, reach Verde in the Islands of the South and buy hull-timber; the timber trade between the isle and Verde has never stopped since.

events.name: The Ferry of the Unbinding
events.summary: The isle's ships carry Selen's companies to the lake port beneath the Parim bluff and feed them through nine years of fighting there.

events.name: The Tide-Seats
events.summary: The isle takes the Charters of Parim with two seats, for Borrak and the Tinta Hills, because its ships owe the common defence more than most lands owe in men.

rivalries.nature: The isle is the first land the western fleets would have to pass, and its queens have watched the West's harbours for four ages.

countries.capitalReason: Borrak is the best natural harbour on the isle and faces the open sea, so the ships of all five houses lie there and the queen who commands them must sit beside them.
countries.today: Orohaf in 4A 1748 is an island queenship of some 300,000 shipwrights, fishers and farmers under Queen Faberra, holding two charter-seats. It builds the Concord's best hulls from Verde's timber, and any fleet crossing from the West must pass its harbours or go far out of its way.

divergence.what: The queen closes the Inner Sea to the western fleets and fights them off Borrak.
divergence.consequence: The Western Crossing must land further south and later, and the isle pays for its loyalty with its ships.

divergence.what: The queen lets the western fleets pass in exchange for the isle being left alone.
divergence.consequence: The Crossing lands on time and in strength, the isle's houses keep their ships, and Parim never forgives the Tide-Oath for keeping its own counsel.

countries.name: Fotan

founding.story: In the century when the Order's grip weakened, a Leren sea-captain, Ostvar, married the daughter of the Aenoran ferry-house that worked the narrowest crossing of the strait, and the two families stretched a chain across the landing and charged the Order's tribute ships to pass. The Order burned their tower twice and never kept them out of it, and the house they founded has held the strait shore and its toll ever since.

roots.story: Fotan's chain is young, but the crossing it closes is the oldest road between the Middle Lands and the North. Before the Ship-Bond of 1A 207 the narrowest crossing of the strait was worked by ferry-families on both shores who had no king and paid no one, and the strait-folk's eldest saying is that a crossing belongs to whoever keeps the boats in repair. The ferry-folk of Deoreh also tell, and nobody has disproved it, that in the deep winters of their grandmothers' grandmothers they heard knocking under the landing, slow and regular, as of picks far below the strait, and that one winter the knocking stopped and never came back. The house of Ostvar grew out of the Order's centuries. In 3A 1104 a Leren sea-captain of that name married the daughter of the Aenoran ferry-house at Deoreh, and when the Order's tribute ships came to cross he cut his ship's anchor-chain from the anchor and stretched it across the landing, and the two families charged the Order to pass. The Order burned their tower twice and never kept them out. From the chain come the lordship's habits: the strait-folk pay their toll to a house, not a crown; Fotan refuses any charter that would make its toll a crown's; it belongs half to the North and half to the Vale and marries into both; and its lords count their descent from a Leren house whose name the margraves of Molot also bear.

sign.device: A black chain drawn taut straight across the field, on a field of red over white.
sign.origin: The chain is the anchor-chain of Ostvar's Leren ship, which he cut from its anchor and stretched across the landing at Deoreh when the Order's tribute ships came to cross in 3A 1104. A link of it is hammered into the toll-post at the landing and the lord of Fotan wears another at his throat; the red over white are the colours of the two families, the Leren captain's and the Aenoran ferry-house's, who held the chain between them.
sign.meaning: The crossing is ours to open and to shut. It promises any ship that pays a safe passage and tells both crowns that the shortest road between the North and the Vale runs under a house that owes neither; since the Toll of Parim the chain has been drawn tighter against Aenoran hulls.

dynasties.name: The House of Ostvar
dynasties.notable: Leren and Aenoran by blood, Leren in its pride and Aenoran in its speech, the house has married across the strait in every generation. Lord Ragnec Ostvar holds the toll in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Knocking Under the Landing
events.summary: The ferry-folk of Deoreh tell that the slow knocking they had heard under the landing in deep winters stops this year and never comes back; nobody on the strait knows what made it.

events.name: The Chain Across the Landing
events.summary: Ostvar and the ferry-house stretch the toll-chain across the landing at Deoreh, and the strait-folk pay their first toll to a house instead of the Order.

events.name: The Charters Refused
events.summary: Fotan refuses the Charters of Parim because a dominion's tolls belong to the common defence, and keeps its strait toll as a free lordship; Harion lets it go, since the strait-folk had fought the Order as hard as anyone.

events.name: The Strait Treaty
events.summary: When Aenor and the North Lands swear the Treaty of the Narrow Strait, Fotan is named in it as neutral ground and its toll is left untouched by both crowns.

events.name: The Toll of Parim
events.summary: A dispute over Fotan's toll on Leren timber is taken to Parim, where the Leren envoys are humiliated; the lord of Fotan takes Lerendor's side and has leaned to Sonargur ever since.

rivalries.nature: The crown has never forgiven the refusal of the Charters, and the Toll of Parim in 4A 1716 made the lordship Lerendor's friend.

countries.capitalReason: Deoreh is the toll-town at the narrowest crossing of the Leren Sea on the Middle Lands side, where the chain can be stretched across the landing and every ship that wants the strait must pass within bowshot of the tower.
countries.today: Fotan in 4A 1748 is a free lordship of some 300,000 strait-folk under Lord Ragnec Ostvar, outside the Concord, living on its strait toll and leaning to Lerendor. Its toll-boats are the best-handled small craft on the strait, and its lord can open or shut the shortest crossing between the North Lands and Aenor.

divergence.what: When Lerendor leaves the Treaty of the Narrow Strait, Fotan opens its landing to the Leren fleet.
divergence.consequence: Lerendor gains a harbour on the Middle Lands side of the strait, and the North's withdrawal becomes an invasion if Sonargur wishes it.

divergence.what: Lord Ragnec draws the chain against every fleet, Leren and Aenoran alike.
divergence.consequence: The strait closes to war for as long as Fotan holds, and both crowns must decide whether the toll-lordship is worth the cost of breaking.

countries.name: Kunhrim

founding.story: The delving-clans had worked the Lunhrim massif since before men had a word for it, and they keep their own count of the years from the first delving, which they do not tell outsiders. To the Aenoran chroniclers Kunhrim begins when the clans cut the Western Gate into the massif's face and opened their galleries to trade with Aen's kingdom; the dwarves say the men only lost a letter when they named the mountain Lunhrim, and that the hold is older than the name.

roots.story: The delving-clans of the Lunhrim massif were one hold of a realm older than any crown of men: the Stone Road, the dwarves' kingdom of deep roads, which joined the western ranges, the Great Wall range and the High Mountains of the North under the floor of the sea, so that a dwarf could walk from the West Lands to the North without seeing the sky. Its seat was the Great Hall of the Deep King, under hills that are now the floor of the Sea of Monsters, and Kunhrim was its eastern gate. In Volgan's war the Damned Spirits rose from beneath the mountains into the roads; the roads under the sea were broken, the sea was let in, and the Great Hall drowned with the spirits inside it. Kunhrim says the Deep King gave the order with his own mouth and that the clans of the massif only carried it out; the western holds say Kunhrim's lords urged it to save their own gate, and the four holds have had no Deep King since. Kunhrim's delvers then fought beside the Grand Alliance and brought down the tunnels the spirits came through. From the drowning comes the hold's character: the sealed Sea-Door at the head of its old road, cut with the names of the last delvers, which no dwarf of the massif may touch; the claim, kept in every lord's oath, that Kunhrim holds the Deep King's last command in trust; the readiness to call the holds to a moot that the western holds always refuse; and a coldness to elves older than the Iron Charter, for the clans say the elves of the Magical Lands watched the Stone Road drown and sent no one down.

sign.device: The Deep King's crown, an iron circlet of square points, above a wavy band of dark blue, on black.
sign.origin: No dwarf has worn the Deep King's crown since the Great Hall drowned, and the crown is shown above a band of sea because it lies under the sea with the hall. Kunhrim's lords have borne it on their banners since the Sea-Door was sealed in 1A 1660, as the hold that says it carried out the last king's command, and they carried it beside Edran's dyed cloak at the crossings in the last war of the First Age.
sign.meaning: The Stone Road had one king and Kunhrim keeps his word. To the holds it is an invitation to a moot and a claim to speak first in it; to the western holds it is the boast of the hold they blame for the drowning, and they say Kunhrim flies the crown it helped to sink.

dynasties.name: The Lords of the Deep Hall
dynasties.notable: The council of clan-elders chooses a Lord of the Deep Hall to speak for the hold at the Western Gate; outsiders deal with him and with nobody else. The office has passed among the clans of Kramast, Hrunord and Dolmerm, and Stulmar of the Kramast clan holds it in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Eastern Gate of the Deep Roads
events.summary: The clans of the Lunhrim massif cut the eastern end of the deep roads that join the great ranges under the dry low country, and the hold becomes the Stone Road's gate towards the east.

events.name: The Western Gate Cut
events.summary: The clans cut the Western Gate and open their galleries to Aenoran trade, and the Lunhrim Notch becomes a packmen's path; the gate faces west because the clans do not care for elves.

events.name: The Sea-Door Sealed
events.summary: When the Damned Spirits come into the Stone Roads, the hold seals the head of its road under the sea with a door cut with the names of the last delvers; the western holds say Kunhrim's lords urged the Letting-In to save their own gate.

events.name: The Delvers at the Crossings
events.summary: The hold's delvers join Edran's Grand Alliance and fight at Dardan under Brunek of the Stone Roads, the western engineer, collapsing the tunnels that the Damned Spirits came through while the giants held the crossings above them.

events.name: The Forged Letters
events.summary: In the war from within, forged letters in the crown's hand accuse the hold of selling iron to the Necromancer; the clans close the Western Gate in anger, and Aenor fights its last war without dwarf iron.

events.name: The Galleries Hold
events.summary: The Order takes the Vale but never the galleries; Kunhrim shelters fugitives of the resistance in its outer halls throughout the occupation and sells the Order nothing.

events.name: The Iron Charter
events.summary: The hold takes the Charters of Parim as a chartered member with one seat, under the Iron Charter: iron for the crown, and no elf on its roads.

events.name: The Lamp Truce
events.summary: The Lord of the Deep Hall swears the Lamp Truce with the hobgoblin king of Burrikkrit and the new Klungori Guard, so that the goblins keep their caves and leave the dwarves' galleries alone.

events.name: The Tunnel Fight
events.summary: When a warren-boss of Burrikkrit sends goblins through an old tunnel, the hold's delvers fight beside the Klungori Guard underground for a winter and bring the tunnel down.

events.name: The Powder Compact
events.summary: Having learned the making of black powder from the western hold of Hrennost, the clans agree to sell their powder to Aenor's crown alone, and it stands in the Kingson Pass forts from that year.

rivalries.nature: An armed truce since 4A 96, kept by the lamp and broken once in the Tunnel Fight; the clans say goblins remember promises only while they are frightened.
The clans do not care for elves, and the Iron Charter keeps every elf off the hold's roads; the elves return the coolness.

countries.capitalReason: Hrakkerm, the iron fort, is the hold's outer hall at the foot of the Western Gate, where carts from the Kingson Vale can reach and the clans can trade without letting anyone into the deep halls; it is the seat of the Iron Charter because that is where the iron is weighed.
countries.today: Kunhrim in 4A 1748 is a hold of some 45,000 dwarves in the delving-clans and 15,000 men who carry and smith for them, under Stulmar, Lord of the Deep Hall, holding one charter-seat under the Iron Charter. Its iron, gold and gems go west, its black powder goes to the crown and nobody else, and its clans can starve any ruler in Parim of iron if they choose.

divergence.what: The Lord of the Deep Hall refuses iron and powder to a ruler in Parim the clans do not hold to be lawful.
divergence.consequence: The Golden Court, the god-king or a western king finds its armouries empty within a year, and the hold must defend the Western Gate against whoever wants its iron badly enough.

divergence.what: The clans sell iron to the western fleets when they land.
divergence.consequence: The Western Crossing is better armed than history allows, and the Iron Charter is broken by the realm that swore it.

countries.name: Burrikkrit

founding.story: When Elzon's Order took the Vale, it needed watchers for the southern range, the unconquered elves beyond it and the South Pass, and it sent goblin warbands into the warm caves under the Cursed Mountains and paid them in plunder. The Order fell and the goblins did not leave; the warrens tell that the Necromancer promised them the whole range, and that a promise outlives the one who made it.

roots.story: The goblins of Burrikkrit came to the Cursed Mountains as the Order's hirelings, and they are not ashamed of it. In 3A 38 Elzon's Order sent goblin warbands from the southern ranges into the warm caves under the mountains to watch the South Pass and the unconquered elves, paid them in plunder and promised them, the warrens say, the whole range for ever. The first warband carried a single shuttered lantern, and its boss set it in the throne-cave of Glimzig and said that while it burned the warren would stand; it has been relit from its own flame at every king's death since, and the hobgoblin kings hold the throne by holding the lantern. When the Necromancer fell, the goblins learned the thing on which their realm stands: that a promise outlives the one who made it, if you are stubborn enough. Nobody could dig them out. From the lantern and the promise come the warrens' customs: the king is the one who keeps the lamp and the biggest who can; a warren whose lamp goes out is finished and its goblins are taken in by others; every bargain, from the Lamp Truce with the dwarves to the smugglers' rate on the under-roads, is sworn with a lit lamp between the parties; and the goblins measure their right to the range not by any charter but by how long nobody has managed to remove them. The dwarves call that theft and the Guard calls it a siege; the warrens call it the promise kept.

sign.device: A shuttered iron lantern with one shutter open on a yellow light, on dark red-brown.
sign.origin: The lantern is the first warband's, set in the throne-cave of Glimzig in 3A 38 and relit from its own flame at every king's death. The Lamp Truce of 4A 96 was sworn over it, carried up to the Accord tower by the hobgoblin king himself, and the warren-bosses paint it on their shields with as many shutters open as they dare, since a shutter open too wide is a boast the king may answer.
sign.meaning: While the lamp burns the warren stands. Half-open, it promises the dwarves and the Guard that the truce holds and promises every goblin that the range is theirs by stubbornness; a closed lantern on a warren's shield means the warren has gone dark and is free to be taken.

dynasties.name: The Hobgoblin Kings of Glimzig
dynasties.notable: The biggest hobgoblin rules, with warren-bosses under him; a king rules until a bigger one throws him out of the throne-cave. The king in 4A 1748 is Dwibrik, who has held the lamp longer than any king the warrens can name.

events.name: The Garrison Caves
events.summary: The Order sends goblin warbands into the caves under the Cursed Mountains and the southern Giant Mountains, and they dig their first warrens round the throne-cave of Glimzig.

events.name: The Lantern of the First Warband
events.summary: The boss of the first warband sets a shuttered lantern in the throne-cave of Glimzig and says the warren will stand while it burns; every king since is relit from it.

events.name: The Promise Kept
events.summary: When the Necromancer falls, the goblins hold their caves against everyone who comes to clear them, and nobody can dig them out.

events.name: The Lamp Truce
events.summary: The hobgoblin king swears the Lamp Truce over a lit lamp with the Lord of the Deep Hall and the Klungori Guard: the goblins keep the caves, the dwarves the galleries, and nobody crosses into the other's dark.

events.name: The Tunnel Fight
events.summary: A warren-boss sends raiders through an old tunnel into the Guard's villages; the Guard and the dwarves fight a winter underground, and the king gives up the boss to have the lamp lit again in 4A 888.

events.name: The Under-Road Sold
events.summary: The king sells a smugglers' guild passage through the old tunnels under the Giant Mountains; the dwarves find out, the guild is never seen again, and the warrens learn to sell the road more quietly.

rivalries.nature: The armed truce of the lamp; the warrens think the dwarves greedy and the dwarves think the goblins thieves, and both are right.
The sworn company exists to watch the warrens, and the warrens know it.

countries.capitalReason: Glimzig, the lamp hall, is the throne-cave deep under the Cursed Mountains, warm and dry and far from any road, where the Order's first warband made its camp; a goblin king lives where nobody can reach him in daylight.
countries.today: Burrikkrit in 4A 1748 is a warren-kingdom of some 75,000 goblins and 10,000 hobgoblins under King Dwibrik, outside the Concord and inside the dwarves' range, held to the Lamp Truce. Its goblins mine, trap and trade salvage at the edges, ride wurghs on the southern roads and make crude powder for the fire-pots they throw in tunnels; its under-roads are the one way through the range that nobody else knows in full.

divergence.what: In the war the king sells the under-roads to the highest bidder: the hosts of the south, the West or the crown.
divergence.consequence: A hidden road through the Great Wall of Aenor opens to whoever pays, and the Lamp Truce ends the day the dwarves find the buyer in their mountain.

divergence.what: The Guard and the dwarves clear the caves before the war.
divergence.consequence: The goblins scatter into the Forests of Darkhere, the under-roads close, and two Concord realms bleed for a victory nobody else notices.

countries.name: Olodor

founding.story: The gnomes of the Deodolor Hills say their eldest holt was dug under an old tree north of the Stone Forest before the War of Men reached the hills, and that its first village-king was crowned by the richest gnomes of the holt with a pot of gold. Men have never found that holt and do not know its name; the year given is the gnomes' own boast, repeated by the one Parim scholar who claims to have heard it.

roots.story: The gnomes of the Deodolor Hills say their first holt was dug under an old tree north of the Stone Forest before the War of Men reached the hills, and that the war taught them the only law they keep. In those years a beaten king of the Vale hid his treasury in the hills, and the gnomes found it and took it; the warlord who came after it took it from them by force, and every man who carried a coin of it away died badly within the year, the warlord first. The gnomes concluded that gold has a memory: given freely it brings fortune back with it, taken it brings ruin. They have kept the account since, and Naisa of the twelve, whom they honour as the keeper of fortune's ledger, is the only god they ask into a holt. The first village-king was the gnome whose pot was fullest of gold freely given, and he was crowned with the rim of his own pot, struck off and beaten round into a circlet, so that his crown was the measure of his luck; every village-king since has been crowned the same way whenever a pot is full. From the account come the holts' customs: a pot of gold left freely on a quarry ledge buys a mason's good fortune; a stolen coin is never kept; a holt that grows too rich gives its gold away before the luck turns; and the gnomes' great fear is not being found but being robbed, which is why they hide so well within a day's walk of Parim.

sign.device: A crown beaten from the gold rim of a cooking-pot, its two handles standing as side-points, on dark green.
sign.origin: The first village-king of Tovodor was crowned with the rim of his own pot, struck off when it was full of gold freely given and beaten round into a circlet, and every crowning since has made a new one the same way. The kings' old rims hang in the king's holt in order, the eldest at the top, and the gnomes cut the pot-rim crown into the doors of their holts where only another gnome knows to look.
sign.meaning: A king is as lucky as what he was given. It promises fortune to anyone who brings gold freely and ruin to anyone who takes it; to the masons of Parim who knock before they cut, it is the sign that they have knocked on the right stone.

dynasties.name: The Village-Kings of Tovodor
dynasties.notable: Every holt has one king, crowned by its gold-crowned, the richest gnomes; the king of Tovodor is the eldest of them, and the holts meet under him only when they are found. The village-king of Tovodor in 4A 1748 is Pebbo.

events.name: The Stolen Treasury
events.summary: A beaten king's treasury hidden in the Deodolor Hills is taken by the gnomes and then by a warlord, and everyone who carries a coin of it away dies within the year; the gnomes conclude that gold has a memory.

events.name: The Quarries Come Close
events.summary: The Stendorler quarries that cut the grey stone for the lake bridges reach within a hundred paces of a holt; the holt's gnomes leave a pot of gold on the quarry ledge, and the quarrymen move their cutting east and prosper.

events.name: The Holts Unfound
events.summary: The Order searches the hills for hidden folk and never finds the holts; the gnomes say the chiromaws were more trouble than the Necromancer.

events.name: The Mason Under the Bridge
events.summary: A Parim mason repairing a bridge pier finds a gnome door in the Stendorler stone and leaves it shut; his family prospers for three generations, and the masons' guild still tells apprentices to knock before they cut.

countries.capitalReason: Tovodor, the king's holt, is the holt of the eldest village-king, dug into the Deodolor Hills where the old trees of the Stone Forest hide its doors and the quarries cannot reach it.
countries.today: Olodor in 4A 1748 is some 12,000 gnomes in hidden holts under their village-kings, within a day's walk of Parim, and almost nobody in Parim knows it. The gnomes mine gold, keep hidden gardens, give luck to anyone who brings them gold freely and ill luck to anyone who takes it, and honour Naisa of the twelve above every other power.

divergence.what: A lord of Parim finds the holts and takes their gold.
divergence.consequence: The holts meet under the king of Tovodor for the first time in living memory, and the lord's house, the gnomes swear, will have ill luck for as long as anyone remembers why.

divergence.what: A ruler of Aenor brings the holts gold freely in the year of the war.
divergence.consequence: The gnomes' luck follows the giver, and the holts offer their tunnels under the Deodolor Hills as a hiding place for whoever the giver chooses.

countries.name: Dunelaeth

founding.story: After Edran's campaign in the Ember Lands the elves who had lived on both sides of the range drew back east of the Great Wall of Aenor, and the hill elves of the western woods were called home to Herrodon. One household refused: it would not leave the Kingdom Forests at the foot of Lunhrim, where its dead lay, and it stayed on the wrong side of the mountains when its kin went east. Herrodon still calls them the lost kin of the west.

roots.story: The elves who lived on both sides of the Great Wall before the First Age ended were hill elves of the western woods, kin of Herrodon, and they buried their dead in the Kingdom Forests at the foot of Lunhrim with a beech planted on each grave, so that the grave would have a voice when the wind came through it. The household of Thamiel is the one that would not leave them. After Edran's campaign in the Ember Lands, in which many elves died for a war they had opposed, the elves of the western woods were called home east of the range, and the household's dead from that campaign were too newly buried to leave. The Eldest answered Herrodon that a beech planted on a grave cannot be carried over the mountains, and the household stayed; Herrodon wrote its name as lost, and the household wrote the queen's as mistaken. From the graves comes everything that makes Dunelaeth what it is: it lives on the wrong side of the mountains because of its dead; it sings the Kindred Song in its old western form because its dead learned it so; it guided the resistance over the Lunhrim Notch under the Order because the grave-beeches showed the way in snow; and it gives the pass road its guides, because a household that keeps graves must keep the roads to them. Each Eldest is buried among the beeches, and the household's quarrel with Herrodon is not about who left whom but about whether the dead can be left at all.

sign.device: A silver beech leaf laid on a green grave-mound, on twilight blue.
sign.origin: At the Staying of 1A 1678 the Eldest sent Herrodon's envoy home with a single leaf from the grave-beeches instead of an answer, and the queen of Herrodon kept it in the book where she wrote the household's name as lost. The household has borne the leaf on the mound since; its guides wore it painted on their cloaks over the Lunhrim Notch on winter nights, so that a fugitive of the resistance would know whom to follow.
sign.meaning: We stay with our dead. It promises the travellers of the pass road guides who will not leave them, and tells Herrodon that the household's answer is still the leaf; a household that took up the leaf for a war would be carrying its dead with it.

dynasties.name: The Eldest of Thamiel
dynasties.notable: The household of a few hundred houses chooses its Eldest from among themselves, and the Eldest speaks for Dunelaeth to men, to dwarves and to Herrodon. Velaeth is Eldest in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Grave-Beeches
events.summary: The household buries its dead of the Ember Lands campaign in the Kingdom Forests and plants a beech on every grave, as the hill elves of the western woods have always done.

events.name: The Staying
events.summary: The household refuses Herrodon's summons home and stays in the Kingdom Forests; the queen of Herrodon writes its name in her hall's book as lost, and the household writes hers in its own as mistaken.

events.name: The Leaf Sent to Herrodon
events.summary: The Eldest sends Herrodon's envoy home with one leaf from the grave-beeches instead of an answer; the queen keeps it in the book where she writes the household's name as lost.

events.name: The Notch Guides
events.summary: Under the Order the household guides fugitives of the resistance over the Lunhrim Notch into the Magical Lands on winter nights, and the Order's forts on the Kingson Pass never learn which way they went.

events.name: The Guides of the Pass Road
events.summary: Under the Accord of the Passes the household becomes the guides of the road to the Kingson Pass, and the forts on both sides pay it in salt and silver.

events.name: The Envoys of Herrodon
events.summary: Herrodon's queen sends envoys to ask the household home a second time; the Eldest feeds them, shows them the graves and sends them back with gifts and no answer.

rivalries.nature: Kin who have argued for an age about who left whom; there is no enmity, only an old reproach on both sides.
The clans of the massif above the forest keep the Iron Charter's rule against elves, and the household keeps off their roads.

countries.capitalReason: Thamiel, the hill, is the household's hall on a rise in the Kingdom Forests above the pass road, near the graves that kept the household in the west, and from it the guides can see every traveller who comes up from the gorge.
countries.today: Dunelaeth in 4A 1748 is one elven household of some 5,000 under its Eldest, Velaeth, outside the Concord, living in the Kingdom Forests and guiding travellers on the road to the Kingson Pass. It is the only elven realm on the Middle Lands side of the range, and the Kindred Song is sung there in an old western form the eastern elves find quaint.

divergence.what: The household answers Herrodon at last and goes east over the pass.
divergence.consequence: The Kingdom Forests are left without guides, and the elves of the Magical Lands gain a household that knows every way men use through the mountains.

divergence.what: The Eldest guides an army over the Lunhrim Notch in the war, for the heir or against him.
divergence.consequence: A host comes through a pass that admits only raiders, and the household chooses a side in a war of men for the first time since the Staying.

countries.name: Aenor Forest

founding.story: The Baelim say that Graulvoa, the oldest stand of their forest, was already standing when the sea first reached the north coast, and the Selen rangers who live round the forest have no story older than the Baelim's low voices in the wood. The great wet forest between Selen, Konori and the Bloody Forest has never been cut, never had a crown and never let a man build in it; the year is only the rangers' guess at the oldest stand, and the Baelim answer questions about years with silence.

roots.story: The Baelim say that their oldest stand, Graulvoa, was already standing when the sea first reached the north coast, and the Selen rangers who live round the forest have no story older than the Baelim's low voices. What the rangers have learned in four ages of watching is a pattern rather than a history. The great wet forest has never been cut and never burned twice: when the Redbark fired its eastern edge in 2A 1120 the Baelim came out and pulled down the raiders' camp trees, and when the Order's woodcutters went in for its giant conifers in 3A 860 not one came back. After each of these the forest kept a silence, a whole year in which no Baelim voice was heard, and where trees had fallen the rangers found the cones of the dead trees gathered and laid closed in rows at the forest's edge, never opened, as if kept for something. The Standing Silence is the rangers' name for those years, and the Baelim's way of life seems to grow from it: they do not grieve aloud; they keep what the dead trees leave; they never share a forest with the ents; and they listen, the rangers think, to something under the roots that is older than the stand. What it is, the Baelim will not say, and the moots have learned not to send anyone in to ask. Selen leaves water at the edge in dry summers, and nobody knows whether the Baelim drink it.

sign.device: A closed black pine-cone, upright, on deep forest green.
sign.origin: The closed cones are those the rangers found laid in rows at the forest's edge after the Burnt Edge and after the cutters who did not return, the cones of the dead trees kept unopened. Selen's rangers have marked the forest's boundary with a painted closed cone since 2A 1121, as a sign to their own people and to the Redbark, and the moots call the forest by it in their books, since the Baelim have never shown a sign of their own.
sign.meaning: What falls is kept, and the forest waits. It tells every axe and every fire that the forest remembers its dead; what the cones are kept for, and whether they will ever open, nobody outside the forest knows.

dynasties.name: The Eldest of Graulvoa
dynasties.notable: The Baelim are named for their stands and their stands for their oldest tree; the Eldest of the oldest stand speaks for the whole forest in its slow moot, and nobody outside has ever heard the moot end. Men call the present Eldest Goarvom.

events.name: The Burnt Edge
events.summary: Redbark raiders set fire to the forest's eastern edge to drive game; the Baelim come out of the wood and pull down the raiders' camp trees, and the Redbark have not lit a fire in the forest since.

events.name: The Cones at the Edge
events.summary: A year after the Burnt Edge, Selen rangers find the cones of the burned trees laid closed in rows along the forest's edge and begin to mark the boundary with a painted closed cone.

events.name: The Cutters Who Did Not Return
events.summary: The Order sends woodcutters to take the forest's giant conifers for its forts; none of them come back, and the Order does not send more.

events.name: The Baelim Speak
events.summary: Selen rangers on the forest edge hear the Baelim's voices for nine nights running after a great storm brings down part of a stand; the moots send a ranger in with an offering of water, and the voices stop.

rivalries.nature: The Redbark hunt at the forest's eastern edge and remember the Burnt Edge; the Baelim remember it too.

countries.capitalReason: Baeldran, the old tree, is Graulvoa, the oldest stand of the forest, where the Eldest stands; the Baelim did not choose a seat, they grew one, and men named it.
countries.today: The Aenor Forest in 4A 1748 is a forest domain without a crown, the largest forest of the Middle Lands and home of some 1,500 Baelim, a slow tree-people unlike the ents of Kilinti, who never share a forest with them. No men live inside it; tzikor flower in its clearings, and Selen's rangers leave water at its edge in dry summers.

divergence.what: An army cuts or burns the forest's edge in the war.
divergence.consequence: The Baelim come out of the wood as they did against the Redbark, slowly and without mercy, and the army learns why no road has ever been made through the north coast.

divergence.what: The Baelim let the people of the Selen edge shelter under the stands when the dead come from the north.
divergence.consequence: The largest forest of the Middle Lands becomes a refuge, and the Baelim speak to men in the moot for the first time anyone remembers.

countries.name: Cursed Lands

founding.story: When Aen's victory ended the War of Men, the Orran-speaking houses that would not kneel to the One Crown withdrew into the grey downs east of the Vale with their cord-mothers, their names knotted on the cords and their tongue. The downs were poor but not yet sour, and the Veiled, as the Vale called them for the hoods their women wore, refused every crown that came after; the land was named the Cursed Lands only after the Black Roots soured it in the Third Age.

roots.story: The Veiled are the eldest heirs of the Low Country, the drowned plain whose Moot of Mothers governed more land than Aenor ever held, and without a crown. Its law was kept on knotted cords, one knot for every field, debt, marriage and death, and when the mothers overdrew the land's magic and the ground sank below the sea, every field the sea took was tied on the Moot's cord as a black knot; the last black knot was tied for the Night of the Sea. The Orran kingdoms that survived on the river valleys kept the cords through the War of Men, and when Aen's victory ended it the houses that would not kneel carried the Moot's cord, the Last Cord, into the eldest barrow of the grey downs. Since then the cord-mothers have kept its count on the Old Tallies, and the Veiled have built their life on the lesson of the black knots: a land must never be asked for more than it gives; a name tied into the mother's cord is never untied, and a name stolen is a knot cut; and the hood their women wear, from which the Vale took its name for them, is the mourning hood for the drowned. The second death of land they suffered taught it again. In 3A 744 the Black Roots of the Necromancer reached the downs, and his attempt to turn the land's magic soured the ground for ever; the Veiled count the sour downs as the second land to die of being asked too much. They stayed, learned to grow roots and mushrooms in it, and refuse every crown, because every crown asks.

sign.device: A grey cord hanging in a loop, tied in one black knot, on sour grey-green.
sign.origin: The black knot is the last tie of the Last Cord, the knot the Moot tied for the Night of the Sea, which lies with the cord in the eldest barrow of the grey downs. The cord-mothers tie a black knot into the cord of every Veiled child at its naming, so that each carries the drowning with her, and the Concord host of the Grey March in 4A 1310 found a black knot tied to the rope of every poisoned well.
sign.meaning: What was taken is never untied. It promises the Veiled that their dead and their drowned are counted, and tells every crown that comes to the downs that it is asking, and that the cord-mothers know what asking does to a land.

dynasties.name: The Cord-Mothers of Morluma
dynasties.notable: The Veiled are ruled by a council of cord-mothers, each keeping the eldest cord of her line, and descent runs through mothers; the Mother of the Eldest Cord speaks for the council. Izkala, daughter of Pelzen, keeps the eldest cord in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Black Knots
events.summary: Through the centuries of the Long Settling every field the sea takes from the Low Country is tied as a black knot on the Moot's cord, and the last black knot is tied for the Night of the Sea.

events.name: The Withdrawal
events.summary: The Orran houses that refuse the One Crown withdraw into the grey downs and the Bloody Forest; the Veiled and the Redbark have counted the same tie as their first since then.

events.name: The Last Cord Laid
events.summary: At the Withdrawal the cord-mothers carry the cord of the old moot into the eldest barrow of the grey downs, and the Veiled keep its count on the Old Tallies from then on.

events.name: The Revolt of the Hoods
events.summary: In the long weakening the Veiled raid the Vale's eastern roads for a generation, and the crown gives up trying to tax the downs.

events.name: The Souring
events.summary: The Black Roots reach the grey downs and the Necromancer's attempt to turn the land's magic sours the ground for ever; the Veiled stay, learn to grow roots and mushrooms in the sour earth, and the Vale names the land cursed.

events.name: The Charters Refused
events.summary: The cord-mothers refuse the Charters of Parim, as they refused every crown before; Harion lets them alone, since the land is not worth an army.

events.name: The Grey March
events.summary: A Concord host marches into the downs to bring the Veiled under charter and turns back after a summer of poisoned wells and empty villages; no host has tried since.

rivalries.nature: The Veiled have rejected the crown since the Peace of the One Crown; the Grey March of 4A 1310 is their proudest tie.

countries.capitalReason: Morluma is the cord-hall deep in the sour ground where no road reaches, chosen because it is the one place on the downs a Concord host would starve before it arrived.
countries.today: The Cursed Lands in 4A 1748 are a council of cord-mothers over some 40,000 Veiled on sour grey badlands, outside the Concord and against it. They speak Orran among themselves, count the years by the ties of the eldest cord, and trade roots and mushrooms at the downs' edge for iron and salt.

divergence.what: The cord-mothers tie the returned heir's name into the eldest cord.
divergence.consequence: For the first time since the Withdrawal the Veiled stand with a king of Aen's line, and their knowledge of the sour ground opens a road the dark does not watch.

divergence.what: The cord-mothers open the downs to the hosts of the south against the crown that has never let them be.
divergence.consequence: The southern host gains a road round the Vale's eastern flank, and the Veiled learn too late what their new friends think of the living.

countries.name: Bloody Forest

founding.story: The Orran houses that refused the One Crown and went north rather than to the downs took to the great red-oak forest above the Konorar, where the bark bleeds red when it is cut. There the Redbark clans have lived ever since by hunting and dyeing leather, ruled by their cord-mothers in peace and by war-chiefs on raids, and they have never taken a charter from any king.

roots.story: The Redbark are the warlike heirs of the Low Country, and their forest is a cord-hall made of trees. When the sea drove the Orran houses east off the drowning plain, those of the Wolf, Bear and Raven clans who would not settle under the valley kings went north into the great red-oak forest above the Konorar and hung their mothers' cords in the oaks. The Redbark tell that the oaks bled when the cords were tied to them and have bled since whenever their bark is cut, because the forest took the drowned into it with their names; the oaks of the forest do run red when cut, and no other red-oak wood in Aoaz does the same. From the cord-trees comes the Redbark's double life: in peace the cord-mothers rule and read the names on the trees; for a raid the moot chooses a war-chief and takes the office back at the peace, as the Low Country did in its wars; a blood-price is paid by tying a knot for the dead into the killer's clan cord; and a feud is ended by the mothers, never by the chiefs. They kept the old tongue and the beast-clans long after the Vale forgot them, and they keep a hunter's grievance: the rivers of the Vale have Orran names, the Redbark say, because those rivers were theirs, and they would take the names back. Under the Order the Necromancer's dead came into the forest and did not come out, and the Redbark say it was because the trees hold the names, and what is already counted cannot be raised.

sign.device: A red oak leaf, stem upward, letting fall one red drop, on black.
sign.origin: The bleeding leaf is the cord-tree's, the oak the Redbark say took the drowned into it with their names. The cord-mothers cut a leaf and a drop into every cord-tree when a new name is tied there, and the war-chiefs carry it painted on a hide on a raid so that the clan's dead go with them; the Selen rangers who burned the cord-trees at the forest's rim in the Red Winter of 4A 1608 learned what the sign meant the next spring.
sign.meaning: The forest bleeds for its dead and its dead are counted. It promises the clans a blood-price for every wrong and tells the Vale that the Redbark have not forgotten the rivers; on a raid it means the war-chief goes with the dead's leave.

dynasties.name: The Clan Moot of Giritren
dynasties.notable: The clans of the Redbark meet at the moot-clearing under the oldest red oak, and the cord-mothers of the clans choose a war-chief for each raid and unmake him when it ends. Tzorek, son of Amaz, is the moot's war-chief in 4A 1748 for a feud that has run three summers.

events.name: The First Cord-Tree
events.summary: Orran houses driven east by the sea hang their mothers' cords in the red oaks of the forest, and the forest keeps the beast-clans and the old tongue long after the valleys forget them.

events.name: The Withdrawal North
events.summary: The northern Orran houses go into the red-oak forest and tie the first tie of the Redbark cords; their kin the Veiled go into the downs.

events.name: The Burnt Edge
events.summary: Redbark hunters fire the edge of the Aenor Forest to drive game, and the Baelim pull down their camp trees; the clans have not hunted in that forest since.

events.name: The Dead in the Red Oaks
events.summary: The Order's dead come into the forest and do not come out; the Redbark tell that their cord-trees hold the names of the dead, and that the Necromancer could not raise what was already counted.

events.name: The Red Winter
events.summary: A Redbark raid burns three Selen glade villages, the rangers burn the cord-trees at the forest's rim, and the feud runs until the cord-mothers and the Wardens exchange hostages in the spring.

events.name: The Reading at the Cord-Trees
events.summary: After the Red Winter the cord-mothers read the names from the burned cord-trees aloud at Giritren and tie them again on new oaks, while the hostages exchanged with Selen listen.

rivalries.nature: Raid and counter-raid at the forest edge since the First Age; the Red Winter of 4A 1608 is the feud both sides still name.
The Burnt Edge of 2A 1120 is remembered by the Redbark as a lesson and by the Baelim as a debt.

countries.capitalReason: Giritren is the moot-clearing under the oldest stand of red oak, where the clans' cord-trees stand and where every Redbark cord was first knotted; the clans live scattered and meet there only for the moot.
countries.today: The Bloody Forest in 4A 1748 is a clan moot of some 90,000 Redbark under their cord-mothers, outside the Concord and against it. They hunt red deer and boar, dye leather, smuggle along the Organ Coast Road and raid the Selen edge when the moot's war-chief needs a name.

divergence.what: The clans guide raiders or an army along the Organ Coast Road beneath the cliffs at low tide.
divergence.consequence: A road that admits only single files at low water carries war into the north of the Vale, and the Redbark get the price they ask from whoever pays it.

divergence.what: The cord-mothers make peace with Selen's moots when the dead come from the north.
divergence.consequence: The oldest feud of the Middle Lands ends in the war, and the forest's hunters join the rangers against something that cannot be tied into any cord.

cities.name: Parim
cities.legend: The bargemen say the bluff was an Orran ford-town before the War of Men, and that the oldest stones of the lower quays still carry Orran marks; the Stone Forest north of the city, they add, is the wood that heard Aen's last horn and stood still, which is why it creaks in a lake fog.
cities.economy: The crown, the Royal Council, the Concord courts, the University of Parim and the Golden Court; grain barges, lake shipping, cloth, glass, books and the sale of offices.

cities.name: Dolepar
cities.legend: Lake sailors hold that Dolepar's deep bay was dug by Aen's hand in a single night so that his ships would never wait on the weather, and the shipwrights still cast a nail into the water before every launching.
cities.economy: The best deep-water harbour of the lake's south lobe; shipyards, the lake fleet and the grain trade to Safeton.

cities.name: Silesire
cities.legend: Where the Great River comes out of the Kingson gorge into the east lobe, the grain-merchants say the river brings everything down from the mountains but news, which always arrives a week late.
cities.economy: Grain port for the Vale's east, the range trade from Kingson, corallus-wardens in the reeds.

cities.name: Kerepael
cities.legend: Edran built the road fortress where the east road leaves the plain for the gorge, and the garrison still sounds a horn at dusk that, the soldiers say, Edran ordered blown until a king of Aen's line came back to stop it.
cities.economy: Garrison town of the east road, wagon yards, the crown's armoury for the eastern dominions.

cities.name: Grafas
cities.legend: The grey ford under the Grano hills where giants once waded across the lake shallows with stone on their backs; the townsfolk keep a giant's footprint in the quay paving and charge travellers to stand in it.
cities.economy: The west-shore lake port; giant-cut stone from Hirolon, wool and cheese from the Hilofrim herders.

cities.name: Hifeco
cities.legend: Under the Moot Tree beside the town Edran was crowned while the capital lay in enemy hands, and the rangers say the oak has not dropped a leaf on a moot day since.
cities.economy: Moot-house of the Weald, the University of Selen, timber and hunting, the ranger companies' musters.

cities.name: Deolofson
cities.legend: The town takes its name from the son of Deolof, the first Pass-Lord, who held the gorge alone for a night when the Order's last host came back for its forts; the vale reads his name first at every Reading of Names.
cities.economy: The only market inside the range: elven silver, herbs and dragon-scale west, iron, grain and glass east; the pass tolls.

cities.name: Torunalos
cities.legend: The High Chief's hall stands above the cairn-fields on the hill from which every crest of the ring can be seen, and the giants say a chief who cannot see the whole ring from his door has no business being chief.
cities.economy: The giants' hall, the cairn-keepers, cattle that haul stone, the harvest-share brought up from Tirlan.

cities.name: Ulmaros
cities.legend: The harbour at the Hilorn mouth was rebuilt after the sea-orcs burned it, under a beacon-cairn the giants raised in a single night; fishermen say the cairn is the only lighthouse in Aoaz that has never needed a fire.
cities.economy: The ring's only landing: fish, trade with Aenor Isle across the Inner Sea.

cities.name: Hilofrim
cities.legend: The herders tell that a giant once carried a whole flock over the Grano Saddle in a winter storm and asked only for the bell of the lead ram, which hangs over the market cross to this day.
cities.economy: Herders' market at the Grano Saddle; wool, cheese and hides; the House of the First Light that serves the herders.

cities.name: Tirbur
cities.legend: The small folk say the morning fog that lies over Tirbur's fields is the giants' breath, laid over the valleys at night to keep the soil soft and the strangers out.
cities.economy: The moot-place of the three valleys; barley, beans, orchards, honey, beer and a dried smoking herb.

cities.name: Arrovez
cities.legend: At the ford of the Aenar the Hundreds raise their kings on the white felt, and the riders say a king who is set down from the felt must cross the ford on foot and never ride it again.
cities.economy: Horse fairs, remounts for the Concord, the king's felt-hall, the ford toll.

cities.name: Ulrono
cities.legend: The Gathering ground is mostly tents and empties every autumn, and the riders say the stone halls in its middle were built by a Horse-Lord who was tired of losing his hall to the wind.
cities.economy: The summer Gathering, the largest horse fair in Aoaz, the horse-barrows of the downs.

cities.name: Hungohon
cities.legend: On the tower wall hangs the helmet of the warren-boss who broke the Lamp Truce, and the Guard's children are told that it shakes on the nights the goblins dig.
cities.economy: The South Pass garrison, the pilgrim escorts and their fees, farming for the sworn company.

cities.name: Hugomon
cities.legend: Hezar built the fort where the southern road enters the Grey Hills, and the march-folk say his towers face south because he was the only man in the Alliance who expected the war to come back.
cities.economy: March fort and garrison, sheep and barley of the Grey Hills, the southern road's trade.

cities.name: Saelori
cities.legend: The Oath of Eight Hearths was sworn at Saelori's fair-ground over eight fires, and the confederacy still lights eight fires on the first night of every fair so that no town can say its hearth was forgotten.
cities.economy: The fairs of Saelori, toll-free trade, the confederacy's treasury.

cities.name: Ollolor
cities.legend: The moot-grove has no walls and no houses; the edge-folk say that a man who sleeps in it wakes a year older and a word wiser, and so nobody sleeps there.
cities.economy: No trade of its own; the Ent-Moot every seventh spring, and the edge-folk's offerings of water.

cities.name: Lotrenri
cities.legend: Where the lake water meets the sea at the Safen mouth, the ship-houses say a drop of the Great Lake reaches every coast of Aoaz, and their captains pour a cup of lake water into the sea on every outward voyage.
cities.economy: Warehouses, grain shipping, the pilgrim fleet south, shipbuilding.

cities.name: Hordorton
cities.legend: The warm spring of Hordorton rose, the Bowl-Bearers say, where Sulethe set down her bowl to rest on the road, and they still break a bowl on the spring-house threshold when a fever leaves the town.
cities.economy: Spring-houses and hospitals, drovers' inns, the crossing of the lake road and the south road.

cities.name: Horlomon
cities.legend: The guild-hall bell was the first thing cast in Horlomon, before the guild-hall had a roof, and the bell-founders say the town grew up round the sound of it.
cities.economy: Bells, glass, cloth, paper, books and ships; the guild library.

cities.name: Borrak
cities.legend: The queens are chosen in the tide-chamber at the harbour's mouth at the turn of the tide, and the isle's grandmothers say a queen chosen on a falling tide will rule a short time and a hard one.
cities.economy: The isle's fleet, the shipwrights who build with Verde's timber, fishing, the tide-chambers.

cities.name: Deoreh
cities.legend: The toll-chain at Deoreh has been broken three times in four ages, and each time the strait-folk melted the broken links into the chain's new anchor, which is why they say the chain grows heavier every century.
cities.economy: The strait toll, toll-boats, ferries and Leren timber.

cities.name: Hrakkerm
cities.legend: The iron fort at the foot of the Western Gate is where the clans weigh their iron before it goes down to Kingson, and the dwarves say a man who argues with the scales will be told the weight of his own head.
cities.economy: The hold's outer hall and market; iron, gold and gems; the Iron Charter's weighing-house; black powder for the crown.

cities.name: Glimzig
cities.legend: The throne-cave's lamp has never gone out since the first warband lit it, and the goblins say a warren lives as long as its lamp burns, which is why the king's lamp has the best guards in the mountain.
cities.economy: Mining, trapping, salvage and the sale of whatever falls into the tunnels; fire-pots and crude powder.

cities.name: Tovodor
cities.legend: Nobody in Parim has ever seen Tovodor, but the masons' guild tells apprentices that a gnome door in the Stendorler stone leads there, and that the luck of the man who leaves it shut lasts three generations.
cities.economy: Gold mining, hidden gardens, and the luck the gnomes give for gold freely brought.

cities.name: Thamiel
cities.legend: The household's hall stands above the graves that kept it in the west, and the elves say that every traveller they guide over the pass road is shown the graves first, so that he knows why the guides stayed.
cities.economy: Guiding on the road to the Kingson Pass, paid in salt and silver by the forts; forest crafts.

cities.name: Baeldran
cities.legend: Graulvoa, the oldest stand, is where the Eldest stands, and the Selen rangers say the moss under it is warm in winter and that the low voices of the stand can be heard there on still nights.
cities.economy: None; the rangers leave water at the forest edge in dry summers.

cities.name: Morluma
